Brucellosis: Ondersterpport Biological Services and the impact on animal health in SA

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Despite getting a R500 million cash injection from Treasury the OBS is not manufacturing crucial vaccines necessary for food security in SA

Summary:
Brucellosis a highly contagious bacterial infection in cattle, goats, sheep, wild animals and humans is a nasty, debilitating illness that’s rapidly spreading through animal populations across South Africa. The most common way people contract it is by drinking unpasteurised milk, but farmers, vets and farm workers are most at risk and many rural vets and farm workers are infected. Brucellosis is extremely difficult to treat in humans and infected animals have to be culled. In humans, unless it’s diagnosed in the first few months it’s almost impossible to treat as it’s an inter-cellular bacteria. It very painful, leaving the victim with chronic fatigue, and severe depression as it attacks the amino acids in the body, wiping out dopamine and serotonin.

The collapse of the State Veterinary services along with the decline of the production of vital medication by the Onderstepoort veterinary services is threatening food security in South Africa. The national herd is extremely unproductive, badly managed and under resourced.

Further information:
Dairy farmers are required to tests for Brucellosis every month but it’s a voluntary test for red meat producers. It’s a notifiable disease and if cattle are infected the herd has to be quarantined and the infected cattle culled. Only after 3 clear tests is the herd cleared and this is very costly to the farmer. In the 80’s South Africa had all but wiped out Brucellosis. There was a rigorous testing and inoculation program across all populations. The state paid private vets to inoculate and testing herds on a regular basis. Communal farming areas were regularly inspected and all inoculation undertaken by the state. This no longer happens. Farmers now have to test and inoculate their own cattle; many don’t either because of cost or ignorance. It’s in the interests of the commercial farmer to test all cattle but poor management on both state and the private sector is the issue.
But to exacerbate the problem the vaccine is no longer available. Ondersterpoort Biological Services is a private run labatory with the State as the only shareholder. It used to supply the whole of Southern Africa but has been in decline over the last 20 years with an increasing lack of capacity. Despite getting a 500 Million cash injection from Treasury in 2014 the laboratories are still in disarray. S19 (the inoculation for Bruceilla) has not been available for the last two years and this vaccine is not manufactured abroad, the feeling is the commercial farmers must just absorb the costs and buy the imported RB51. They also have been in short supply of a number of other crucial products like the TB testing kits, tetanus, Ecoli, blue tongue, 3 day Fever, Rift Valley Fever, Pasturella, and Abscess treatments, and there are no alternative drugs for theses illnesses
Cattle must be inoculated with S19 between 3 and 6 months old, after that the inoculation gives the animal a false positive reading. After that a drug called RB51 is the only one that can be used. But RB51 needs to be injected more frequently. Fortunately RB51 is imported but costs 5 times as much as the once off inoculation. Ondersterpoort the State biological services are the only manufacturers and suppliers of S19 and for the past 5 years they have not been producing it regularly. Vets in the Vryberg region have been waiting for 2 years to treat local herds.
Russel Garnett a farmer in the Vryberg region says for the last 5 years he starts sourcing S19 for months in advance phoning across the country even Namibia to source sufficient supplies. This year he could source any. He says he will use RB51 if he can’t get any but it’s an expensive option. You can’t contract brucellosis from meat products and so red meat producers take more chances, but once a herd is infected it spreads like wild fire. Also stud stock has to be culled and they only get the price for the meat and not the true value of the animal.
Russel’s father Chris contracted Brucellosis and spent 5 years in bed severely depressed. His vet also has Brucellosis and keeps being infected. But the people most at risk are the farm workers who often fall ill and then just leave the farms and are unlikely to know what ever happened to them as clinics would not be testing for Brucellosis.
There are major problems in the State veterinary services with shortages of both vets as well as resources. Plus each province runs show so there are major disparities across the country and there is not one protocol of testing and vaccinating. Infected animals cross provincial borders so even if the Western Cape has the strongest program they are still at risk from infection.

Press Release:


Brucellosis Threat
An infectious disease caused by the Brucella bacterium is out of control in South African beef herds. It is also threatening our dairy herds and wreaks long-term health havoc in the lives of people who contract it. The effects of Brucellosis have almost crippled many farmers barely managing to keep afloat in the face of nationwide drought. Carte Blanche asks: why isn’t the state-owned laboratory producing enough vaccine against this infection?


Script:


Brucellosis, or Undulant fever, and is totally out of control in the South African cattle herds.
Link: “Alarmingly this disease isn’t only limited to animals it can also be transferred to humans through the consumption of unpasteurised cows and goats milk. It’s a debilitating disease that often goes un-detected
Script: Chris Garnett thinks he contracted Brucellosis from assisting a heifer that aborted
Chris “For me it felt like the end of the world I didn’t think I was going to recover. It was almost 5 years and I think the worst part of it was the severe depression.
Script: The brucella bacterium is an intercellular organism carried in a cow’s uterus causing it to abort spreading millions of bacteria and infecting both animals and people. If the first abortion is missed cattle can then carry to term infecting their calves and milk. Private Vet Riaan Putter says there is an extremely high rate of infection amongst vets
Riaan Putter “Obviously Vets farmers and farm workers are at risk because they assist these animals with calvings because of the placental fluids and the placenta and the foetus itself contains high numbers of these bacteria there is also a risk through raw unpasteurised milk, more so in children that is also a possibility although pasteurised milk is completely safe.
Script: And there is a growing trend to drink unpasteurised milk. Irene dairy farm has been selling raw milk for the last 100 years but they go to great lengths to test both their workers and cattle regularly.
Henry “Nutritionally it is far superior to pasteurised milk but it has to be certified raw milk and because the testing and controls are not what they used to be it is just far more important for the consumer itself they must find out where the milk is coming from they do need to satisfy themselves that it is certified clean and healthy
Chris “It’s very painful in the joints especially in the wrists you become very lethargic, it’s actually even difficult to even go to the toilet, difficult to sleep, there is no having a normal life at all
Script: Chris suffered from undulating fever and was misdiagnosed with flu and depression
Chris Garrett “The problem with diagnosing it 6 months after contracting it is by then it is chronic, and because its inter cellular the only way you can really kill the bacillus is by killing the cell. So where it is quite easy to treat in the acute stages it’s virtually impossible to treat in the chronic stage. They put me on the antibiotics which lasted 6 months
Script: Brucellosis, TB and polio can all be contracted through drinking unpasteurised milk and so the dairy industry strictly controls milk doing monthly tests. Ian Gerber is a dairy farmer in Hoekvile in the Southern Cape, had 1250 cattle last November.
Ian Gerber ”They do a test on the milk and that is the first thing that shows you, you might be positive and then the state vet contacted me and they arrange to take blood samples from the cows
Link: “There is no cure for Brucellosis so when a cow is identified as having been infected it and its calves are culled and the entire herd is also placed under quarantine
Script: Ian had to cull 700 of his prime dairy cows
Ian Gerber “I saw 170 cows leaving the farm on trucks that was heart broken
Script: And it’s a nightmare that isn’t going to go away any time soon, it can take up to 3 years to get a clean herd and the quarantine will only get lifted 2 years after that, it’s extremely costly for the farmer.
Ian Gerber “it was a hard knock for us as a family, we produce 35000 litres a day and currently we are producing 15000 litres a day, and the bottom line is that it just doesn’t pay the bills
Script: Brucellosis is a crisis that has been allowed to get completely out of control, farmers are suffering huge financial loses getting a quarter of the value of their animal when they cull them prematurely. 30 years ago South Africa had almost eradicated it says Danie Odendaal of the Veterinary Network
Danie “look at the Highveld areas the main beef cattle producing areas it’s basically out of control. If you look at our coastal areas where most of our dairy cattle are, there we are still in control but we are on the brink of getting out of control because of the movement of animals.
Script: And the drought is making things worse, animals are sold off to areas where grazing is good, and because there is no control of animals crossing provincial borders, the disease is spreading. Beef cattle were brought into Hoekvil from the Free State to fatten for the market. The neighbouring farm lost 850 cows, and they are still trying to work out exactly how the disease spread from one farm to the other.
Link: Dairy farmers are required to frequently test their herds but it’s a voluntary system for Beef farmers, that means Brucellosis can often go undetected for a long periods of time and infections can spread like wild fire
Danie “On a beef cattle side we don’t know where we stand with Brucellosis, the cases we have reported here is where farmers sought the advice of a vet so there are still 100’s of other farmers that we don’t know of
Script: It’s a notifable disease and by law all cattle have to be vaccinated, but many farmers are ignorant, or they simply can’t get their hands on the vaccine. Chris’s son Russell, says he has been known to drive over 400 kms just to lay his hands on the Strain 19 vaccine
Russell Garnett “I spoke to my vet, and I spoke to the Co-op and initially they said to me there is absolutely none available, and they have got a list of over 200 farmers that are enquiring about it and who are on their waiting list, for the last 9 months according to the records at the co-op in Vryburg none has been available.
Script: Russell breeds cattle in prime beef country just outside Vryburg in the North West, and is acutely aware of the dangers of brucellosis having taken over the running of the farm at 20 when his father fell ill
Russell Garnett “If we can’t get hold of the vaccine it means that many more people can get infected. I am concerned for my health; I am concerned for the health of anybody who works on my farm
Script: He spends months trying to source vaccine contacting co-ops across the country in an effort to get enough.
Russell Garnett “The tricky thing is that you have to vaccinate your heifers between the ages of 4 months and 8 months. I have a 3 month breeding season so there is only 1 month in which I can vaccinate all my heifers, it’s crucial that I get the vaccine when I need. In 2013 there was absolutely none available.
Script: The State vaccinates communal and emerging farmer’s herds, but Bernard Nneelang Manager of Animal Health says they also don’t have vaccine.
Bernard “We are sitting on a time bomb which means that you know the disease is going to spread. They are saying they have got some budgetary constraints so we don’t know when this is going to be resolved.
Script: But the problem is the most difficult to control in the communal herds.
Bernard “It is difficult to contain the disease because in the case of quarantining the area it is impossible so we don’t have camps. Cows can move more than 20kms without anything stopping them
Script: And some farmers aren’t toeing the line, often not notifying State vets of an outbreak.
Russell Garnett “There is serious stigma attached to having serious diseases in a cattle herd because it makes it very difficult to sell your cattle especially breeding stock and they try and hide it because it has a massive effect on their bottom line.
Link: S19 is cheaper but for years it’s been unavailable for long periods of time this is the commercial alternative RB51 but it is 4 times more expensive
Script: Onderstepoort Biological Services, a private company with the State as the major shareholder is the sole supplier of major vaccines. It’s been in decline for many years, and vaccines production has been intermittent, leaving farmers and their animals stranded. In 2014 the State injected R500 million to upgrade the facilities.
Danie “The production units were shut down and an unacceptable thing was they didn’t produce vaccine for the period of time while the upgrades is going to take place. I think it is unheard of, they are the only guys that have registration in SA if they couldn’t produce it they could have imported it
Script: OBP would not schedule an interview with us but via email said “OBP experienced frequent equipment breakdowns due to decaying old equipment which has never been serviced or replaced since late 1960’s. The majority of key equipment has been replaced and the company is in full production. We have 14 000 units in stock which are currently being distributed to all points of sale across the country. And State services will get stock anytime next week.
But it’s too little too late, a minimum of 800 000 vaccines were needed before July to be effective. , Major co-ops like VKB said across their 50 branches they have enough for only 2100 cattle, and AFGRI’s 63 branches, have been battling to get sufficient stock since April.
Danie “What facility can be out of stock for 2 years on a vaccine like Blue Tongue, they are the only producers of that broad spectrum vaccine in the world. To me it’s totally unacceptable.
Script: We turned to the Minister of Agriculture Senzeni Zokwana for answers.
John “There does seem to be an acknowledgement by your department that in some ways OBP have dropped the ball particularly as far as the development of S19 is concerned.
Minister Zokwana” Remember no organization would meet its target which is not funded properly and to me the funding came late, a bit late because by that time a number of things may have happened they have lost the best of their own scientists and they have lost their facilities.
Script: The Minister admits we have a crisis but says there is a Veterinary strategy in place. But Danie says disease is a real-time thing and needs immediate action, which just isn’t happening.
Danie “We have done the workshops right through the country we have a veterinary strategy which is a nice document now we want action plans with people dates and schedules
Script: And it’s only the state that has the resources to eradicate this, and in the mean-time farmers like Ian Gerber are carrying the burden.
Danie “We can’t live with it it’s too big a danger to society. So Brucellosis must be eradicated”

Link: Dairy farmers are required to frequently test their herds but it’s a voluntary system for Beef farmers, that means Brucellosis can often go undetected for a long periods of time and infections can spread like wild fire Danie “On a beef cattle side we don’t know where we stand with Brucellosis, the cases we have reported here is where farmers sought the advice of a vet so there are still 100’s of other farmers that we don’t know of Script: It’s a notifable disease and by law all cattle have to be vaccinated, but many farmers are ignorant, or they simply can’t get their hands on the vaccine. Chris’s son Russell, says he has been known to drive over 400 kms just to lay his hands on the Strain 19 vaccine Russell Garnett “I spoke to my vet, and I spoke to the Co-op and initially they said to me there is absolutely none available, and they have got a list of over 200 farmers that are enquiring about it and who are on their waiting list, for the last 9 months according to the records at the co-op in Vryburg none has been available. Script: Russell breeds cattle in prime beef country just outside Vryburg in the North West, and is acutely aware of the dangers of brucellosis having taken over the running of the farm at 20 when his father fell ill Russell Garnett “If we can’t get hold of the vaccine it means that many more people can get infected. I am concerned for my health; I am concerned for the health of anybody who works on my farm Script: He spends months trying to source vaccine contacting co-ops across the country in an effort to get enough. Russell Garnett “The tricky thing is that you have to vaccinate your heifers between the ages of 4 months and 8 months. I have a 3 month breeding season so there is only 1 month in which I can vaccinate all my heifers, it’s crucial that I get the vaccine when I need. In 2013 there was absolutely none available. Script: The State vaccinates communal and emerging farmer’s herds, but Bernard Nneelang Manager of Animal Health says they also don’t have vaccine. Bernard “We are sitting on a time bomb which means that you know the disease is going to spread. They are saying they have got some budgetary constraints so we don’t know when this is going to be resolved. Script: But the problem is the most difficult to control in the communal herds. Bernard “It is difficult to contain the disease because in the case of quarantining the area it is impossible so we don’t have camps. Cows can move more than 20kms without anything stopping them Script: And some farmers aren’t toeing the line, often not notifying State vets of an outbreak. Russell Garnett “There is serious stigma attached to having serious diseases in a cattle herd because it makes it very difficult to sell your cattle especially breeding stock and they try and hide it because it has a massive effect on their bottom line. Link: S19 is cheaper but for years it’s been unavailable for long periods of time this is the commercial alternative RB51 but it is 4 times more expensive Script: Onderstepoort Biological Services, a private company with the State as the major shareholder is the sole supplier of major vaccines. It’s been in decline for many years, and vaccines production has been intermittent, leaving farmers and their animals stranded. In 2014 the State injected R500 million to upgrade the facilities. Danie “The production units were shut down and an unacceptable thing was they didn’t produce vaccine for the period of time while the upgrades is going to take place. I think it is unheard of, they are the only guys that have registration in SA if they couldn’t produce it they could have imported it Script: OBP would not schedule an interview with us but via email said “OBP experienced frequent equipment breakdowns due to decaying old equipment which has never been serviced or replaced since late 1960’s. The majority of key equipment has been replaced and the company is in full production. We have 14 000 units in stock which are currently being distributed to all points of sale across the country. And State services will get stock anytime next week. But it’s too little too late, a minimum of 800 000 vaccines were needed before July to be effective. , Major co-ops like VKB said across their 50 branches they have enough for only 2100 cattle, and AFGRI’s 63 branches, have been battling to get sufficient stock since April. Danie “What facility can be out of stock for 2 years on a vaccine like Blue Tongue, they are the only producers of that broad spectrum vaccine in the world. To me it’s totally unacceptable. Script: We turned to the Minister of Agriculture Senzeni Zokwana for answers. John “There does seem to be an acknowledgement by your department that in some ways OBP have dropped the ball particularly as far as the development of S19 is concerned. Minister Zokwana” Remember no organization would meet its target which is not funded properly and to me the funding came late, a bit late because by that time a number of things may have happened they have lost the best of their own scientists and they have lost their facilities. Script: The Minister admits we have a crisis but says there is a Veterinary strategy in place. But Danie says disease is a real-time thing and needs immediate action, which just isn’t happening. Danie “We have done the workshops right through the country we have a veterinary strategy which is a nice document now we want action plans with people dates and schedules Script: And it’s only the state that has the resources to eradicate this, and in the mean-time farmers like Ian Gerber are carrying the burden. Danie “We can’t live with it it’s too big a danger to society. So Brucellosis must be eradicated” Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Brucellosis: Ondersterpport Biological Services and the impact on animal health in SA (4836 ) lizfish@iafrica.com 05 September 2016

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Despite getting a R500 million cash injection from Treasury the OBS is not manufacturing crucial vaccines necessary for food security in SA
metadata.Summary: Brucellosis a highly contagious bacterial infection in cattle, goats, sheep, wild animals and humans is a nasty, debilitating illness that’s rapidly spreading through animal populations across South Africa. The most common way people contract it is by drinking unpasteurised milk, but farmers, vets and farm workers are most at risk and many rural vets and farm workers are infected. Brucellosis is extremely difficult to treat in humans and infected animals have to be culled. In humans, unless it’s diagnosed in the first few months it’s almost impossible to treat as it’s an inter-cellular bacteria. It very painful, leaving the victim with chronic fatigue, and severe depression as it attacks the amino acids in the body, wiping out dopamine and serotonin. The collapse of the State Veterinary services along with the decline of the production of vital medication by the Onderstepoort veterinary services is threatening food security in South Africa. The national herd is extremely unproductive, badly managed and under resourced.
metadata.Further information: Dairy farmers are required to tests for Brucellosis every month but it’s a voluntary test for red meat producers. It’s a notifiable disease and if cattle are infected the herd has to be quarantined and the infected cattle culled. Only after 3 clear tests is the herd cleared and this is very costly to the farmer. In the 80’s South Africa had all but wiped out Brucellosis. There was a rigorous testing and inoculation program across all populations. The state paid private vets to inoculate and testing herds on a regular basis. Communal farming areas were regularly inspected and all inoculation undertaken by the state. This no longer happens. Farmers now have to test and inoculate their own cattle; many don’t either because of cost or ignorance. It’s in the interests of the commercial farmer to test all cattle but poor management on both state and the private sector is the issue. But to exacerbate the problem the vaccine is no longer available. Ondersterpoort Biological Services is a private run labatory with the State as the only shareholder. It used to supply the whole of Southern Africa but has been in decline over the last 20 years with an increasing lack of capacity. Despite getting a 500 Million cash injection from Treasury in 2014 the laboratories are still in disarray. S19 (the inoculation for Bruceilla) has not been available for the last two years and this vaccine is not manufactured abroad, the feeling is the commercial farmers must just absorb the costs and buy the imported RB51. They also have been in short supply of a number of other crucial products like the TB testing kits, tetanus, Ecoli, blue tongue, 3 day Fever, Rift Valley Fever, Pasturella, and Abscess treatments, and there are no alternative drugs for theses illnesses Cattle must be inoculated with S19 between 3 and 6 months old, after that the inoculation gives the animal a false positive reading. After that a drug called RB51 is the only one that can be used. But RB51 needs to be injected more frequently. Fortunately RB51 is imported but costs 5 times as much as the once off inoculation. Ondersterpoort the State biological services are the only manufacturers and suppliers of S19 and for the past 5 years they have not been producing it regularly. Vets in the Vryberg region have been waiting for 2 years to treat local herds. Russel Garnett a farmer in the Vryberg region says for the last 5 years he starts sourcing S19 for months in advance phoning across the country even Namibia to source sufficient supplies. This year he could source any. He says he will use RB51 if he can’t get any but it’s an expensive option. You can’t contract brucellosis from meat products and so red meat producers take more chances, but once a herd is infected it spreads like wild fire. Also stud stock has to be culled and they only get the price for the meat and not the true value of the animal. Russel’s father Chris contracted Brucellosis and spent 5 years in bed severely depressed. His vet also has Brucellosis and keeps being infected. But the people most at risk are the farm workers who often fall ill and then just leave the farms and are unlikely to know what ever happened to them as clinics would not be testing for Brucellosis. There are major problems in the State veterinary services with shortages of both vets as well as resources. Plus each province runs show so there are major disparities across the country and there is not one protocol of testing and vaccinating. Infected animals cross provincial borders so even if the Western Cape has the strongest program they are still at risk from infection.
